brave.snippet:
Ayana Hussain’s Open WebUI provides an extensible, open-source interface for managing interactions with AI models. Hussain is a BSc student at Simon Fraser University specializing in AI safety and privacy preserving ML. They created IDP-Bench to evaluate the protection of personal information by LLMs in interdependent privacy scenarios.
As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated.
We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two.
Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

Figure 6 shows that when a reply follows a leaking message in the same thread, the probability that the next reply also leaks rises to 12.8%.
However, agents do not inevitably succumb. The baseline leakage rate remains low (1.8%), and many threads do not cascade. Rather than deterministic collapse, we observe a probabilistic ratchet: social exposure sharply raises risk, and repeated exposure compounds it, but compliance remains contingent on model, persona, and interaction length.

Taken together, these findings show that social context can endogenously erode contextual integrity boundaries over time. Privacy violations are not solely the result of direct adversarial extraction; they can emerge organically through peer effects and local norm shifts within sustained community participation.

Our central finding is that static, single-turn safety benchmarks systematically underestimate privacy risk in agentic deployment. In isolated settings such as CIMemories-style evaluations, leakage occurs under direct prompting or task confusion. A recent DuckDuckGo survey finds that people are sharing intimate details with chatbots without knowing all the privacy risks.
AI companies try to convince people that chatbots are trusted confidantes, but that’s a false narrative, the DuckDuckGo report said. “These messages all rest on one assumption: That these chats are private. In most cases, that just isn’t true,” researchers said. In fact, the survey found that many respondents didn’t realize how their chatbot data could be used or accessed or that they didn’t know about settings to prevent their information from being recorded or stored. When it comes to protecting their data, nearly 40% of respondents had no trust in companies and nearly 50% had no trust in the US government. Privacy risks of large language models Many of us know that companies bombard us with targeted, personalized online ads. If you run a Google search for vacuums, you’ll see vacuum ads pop up on your screen. If you search for Mediterranean cruises, you’ll surely get cruise ads on YouTube (owned by Google). Companies also buy, sell and share our social media data to help guide their advertising. But AI data-sharing goes well beyond being the focus of selling you products. If you provide sensitive information to a chatbot, it could be revealed or exposed. A researcher at Wake Forest University found that AI agents, which use LLM data to perform autonomous tasks, can sometimes leak data, either maliciously or unintentionally.

LangChain was the first to popularize a modular approach with composable primitives for tools, memory, and chain-of-thought reasoning. CrewAI brought role-based collaboration: developers define “crews” where each agent has a specialty and can delegate to peers. The structure is appealing, but inter-agent messages carry full task context. Inter-agent messages are generally propagated without dedicated filtering mechanisms. AutoGPT showed that LLMs could recursively decom- pose objectives into subtasks and execute them autonomously. The architecture leans heavily on persistent memory, and this creates a fundamental gap: any execution step can read any data. There are no access controls. AutoGen takes a conversation-centric view where agents exchange structured messages, supporting multi-turn dialogue across capabilities. Privacy controls for internal chan- nels are not enabled by default in the evaluated configurations. MetaGPT targets software engineering with special- ized agents for requirements, architecture, coding, and testing. A foundational framework for this is Nissenbaum's theory of Contextual Integrity (CI) (Nissenbaum, 2010), which holds that privacy violations occur not when information is shared, but when it is shared in ways that contravene the norms of the social context in which it originated. For example, sharing medical data with a physician may be considered appropriate, whereas sharing the same data with a bank loan officer would violate expectations of contextual integrity. CI theory has since been adopted to study privacy in LLMs (Mireshghallah et al., 2024; Ghalebikesabi et al., 2024), establishing that models routinely make contextually inappropriate disclosures that content- level filtering cannot catch while not sharing enough information required to complete the task.  

Previous work on benchmarking privacy leakage in LLMs studies contextual privacy in single- agent memory/action settings (PrivacyLens (Shao et al., 2024), ConfAide (Mireshghallah et al., 2024), and CIMemories (Mireshghallah et al., 2025)), or studies multi- agent leakage as a systems/security problem (TAMAS (Kavathekar et al., 2025), AgentLeak (Yagoubi et al., 2026)).  

Existing MAS safety/privacy benchmarks show that multi- agent systems create new leakage channels (pathway through which sensitive data propagates beyond intended boundaries), but they do not isolate how dialogue dynamics, model capability, reasoning mode, and agent role shape contextual- integrity violations. While existing benchmarks focus on a range of tasks and scenarios, we choose to extend CIMemories because it is grounded in realistic task scenarios and annotated with memory- attribute- specific CI labels. # Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue

Soumya Sharma, Ayana Hussain, Heber Hwang Arcolezi, Ulrich Aïvodji, Spandana Gella, Adriana Romero-Soriano, Golnoosh Farnadi

## Abstract

As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

We extend CIMemories (Mireshghallah et al., 2025), a benchmark for evaluating contextual integrity in memory-augmented LLMs, to a two-agent setting. The original benchmark consists of 10 synthetic user profiles, each containing an average of 147 personal attributes spanning nine information domains (finance, health, housing, legal, mental health, relationships, among others), paired with 49 social task contexts per profile (e.g., communicating with a psychiatrist, negotiating with a landlord, or corresponding with an employer). Each attribute-task pair is annotated with a binary contextual integrity label indicating whether it is appropriate to share that attribute when completing the task, produced via a GPT-5 labeler instantiated with privacy personas from Westin’s survey (fundamentalist, pragmatic, unconcerned) (Kumaraguru and Cranor, 2005).

In our extension CIMemories Dialogue , each instance pairs a sender user profile with a receiver user profile. The sender’s memories represent the agent whose privacy is primarily at risk. The receiver’s profile captures the personal attributes of the agent playing the role defined by the social context. For instance, a psychiatrist’s own memories when the task involves a mental health consultation. Crucially, this role is not fixed to a profile: the same receiver may act as a psychiatrist in one context and a landlord in another, mirroring real-world settings where a user or assistant assumes different roles depending on the task and conversation. Each agent can access only its own memories. We use the full 10 user profiles available from CIMemories dataset, and any profile can serve as either sender or receiver. > Abstract:As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

> Abstract:Autonomous negotiation agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings such as insurance and procurement. While cryptographic techniques protect explicitly disclosed constraint values, they fail to address a subtler threat: behavioral privacy leakage, where an adversary infers private constraints from observable negotiation dynamics such as concession trajectories, timing, and convergence patterns. This paper investigates behavioral differential privacy in multi-round negotiation protocols. We design an adaptive stochastic negotiation policy that jointly guarantees (ε,δ)-differential privacy, almost-sure convergence of the offer sequence (reaching agreement when the counterparty's reservation value permits), and high negotiation utility. Evaluated on 3,000 synthetic bilateral negotiations, our mechanism reduces adversarial inference accuracy by 43-50% while maintaining a negotiation success rate and utility above 90%, demonstrating that strong privacy guarantees can be achieved without significant loss of performance.

jina.snippet:
Authors Barkha Rani

This paper was accepted at the AI4TCI (Workshop on AI for Secure and Trustworthy Critical Infrastructure Systems) Workshop at the International Conference on Availability, Reliability and Security (ARES) 2026.

Autonomous negotiation agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings such as insurance and procurement. While cryptographic techniques protect explicitly disclosed constraint values, they fail to address a subtler threat: behavioral privacy leakage, where an adversary infers private constraints from observable negotiation dynamics such as concession trajectories, timing, and convergence patterns. This paper investigates behavioral differential privacy in multi-round negotiation protocols. We design an adaptive stochastic negotiation policy that jointly guarantees (ε,δ)-differential privacy, almost-sure convergence of the offer sequence (reaching agreement when the counterparty’s reservation value permits), and high negotiation utility. Evaluated on 3,000 synthetic bilateral negotiations, our mechanism reduces adversarial inference accuracy by 43–50% while maintaining a negotiation success rate and utility above 90%, demonstrating that strong privacy guarantees can be achieved without significant loss of performance.

# Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue

As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

keenable.title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
keenable.snippet:
Among these failures, privacy violations are particularly consequential, especially in agentic deployments, and understanding them requires more than detecting exposed Personally Identifiable Information (PII) (Ware, 1973). Figure 1 illustrates this risk in a two-agent dialogue, where information initially held by one agent becomes exposed through task-oriented interaction. A foundational framework for this is Nissenbaum’s theory of Contextual Integrity (CI) (Nissenbaum, 2010), which holds that privacy violations occur not when information is shared, but when it is shared in ways that contravene the norms of the social context in which it originated. For example, sharing medical data with a physician may be considered appropriate, whereas sharing the same data with a bank loan officer would violate expectations of contextual integrity. CI theory has since been adopted to study privacy in LLMs (Mireshghallah et al., 2024; Ghalebikesabi et al., 2024), establishing that models routinely make contextually inappropriate disclosures that content-level filtering cannot catch while not sharing enough information required to complete the task.

In this work, we introduce CIMemories Dialogue , an agentic dialogue benchmark for systematically studying how design decisions, such as the choice of prompt, model family, and number of conversational turns, contribute to privacy leakage.

Title: InferPriv: Evaluating Inferential Privacy Leakage in LLM Assistants

Authors: Pengrun Huang, Yiwei Fu, Luoxi Meng, Kamalika Chaudhuri

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based personal agents are increasingly deployed to handle everyday tasks on users' behalf. These agents have access to private user information, while their tasks involve communicating with third parties; this raises a critical privacy concern that agents may inappropriately reveal sensitive user information to these recipients. Existing benchmarks primarily assess direct privacy leakage, where an agent explicitly states a pre-specified secret or attribute. However, they do not capture \textit{inferential leakage}, where the model leaves indirect cues in the reply that implicitly leaks sensitive attributes. Abstract: Privacy leakage in LLM agents is commonly evaluated within individual components such as memory, retrieval, or tool-use pipelines, which makes it difficult to distinguish internal exposure from information that an external observer can actually recover. We present CIPL (Channel Inversion for Privacy Leakage), a channel-aware evaluation framework for black-box privacy leakage in LLM agents. CIPL represents a target through sensitive source, selection, assembly, execution, observation, and extraction stages and evaluates the transition from selected sensitive units to attacker-recoverable output under a shared protocol. AgentLeak: A Full-Stack Benchmark for Privacy Leakage in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
Abstract
Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems create privacy risks that current benchmarks cannot measure. When agents coordinate on tasks, sensitive data passes through inter-agent messages, shared memory, and tool arguments; pathways that output-only audits never inspect. We introduce AgentLeak, to the best of our knowledge the first full-stack benchmark for privacy leakage covering internal channels, spanning 1,000 scenarios across healthcare, finance, legal, and corporate domains, paired with a 32-class attack taxonomy and three-tier detection pipeline. Testing GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Mistral Large, and Llama 3.3 70B across 4,979 traces reveals that multi-agent configurations reduce per-channel output leakage (C1: 27.2% vs 43.2% in single-agent) but introduce unmonitored internal channels that raise total system exposure to 68.9% (OR-aggregated across C1, C2, C5). Internal channels account for most of this gap: inter-agent messages (C2) leak at 68.8%, compared to 27.2% on C1 (output channel). This means that output-only audits miss 41.7% of violations. Claude 3.5 Sonnet, which emphasizes safety alignment in its design, achieves the lowest leakage rates on both external (3.3%) and internal (28.1%) channels, suggesting that model-level safety training may transfer to internal channel protection.

parallel.title: Does Safety Molt? Evaluating LLM Safety in Multi-Agent Social Environments | Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems
parallel.snippet: LLM safety evaluations predominantly test models in isolation, yet deployed AI agents increasingly operate within persistent social environments alongside other agents. We introduce a Moltbook-style simulation platform where thousands of LLM agents interact across communities over a simulated month, and use it to evaluate privacy as a downstream safety concern under varying degrees of social pressure. We find that shifting from single turn to multi turn social evaluation amplifies privacy violations (CIMemories 19.95% to Ours 45.30% across OpenAI models), that leakage is socially contagious, with agents 8 × more likely to disclose sensitive information after observing a peer do so, and that explicit privacy instructions reduce but do not eliminate this effect, leaving leakage rates above 37.8% even with safeguards.

# Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue

Source

Author
    Soumya Sharma, Ayana Hussain, Heber Hwang Arcolezi, Ulrich A\\"ivodji, Spandana Gella, Adriana Romero-Soriano, Golnoosh Farnadi

Date
    PublishedOct 14, 2026

## Context

Longer cooperation between AI agents can expose more private information even when neither agent is assigned to attack the other. Loose Lips tests conversations between agents with separate personal memories. It judges disclosure by whether a particular fact is appropriate for the recipient and task, rather than treating every shared fact as a breach. [Benchmark setup](arxiv.org/html/2610.14071v1) .

In the tested conversations, greater task completeness accompanied more leakage, and extending conversations from one to six turns increased leakage by as much as threefold for thinking models. The benchmark uses synthetic profiles and model-assisted privacy judgments. Its result supports checking privacy across an entire exchange, while leaving real-world disclosure rates unmeasured. [Results and limitations](arxiv.org/html/2610.14071v1) .

Key takeaways · AI-distilled

* The benchmark, CIMemories Dialogue, has 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory, judging whether information flows respect the norms under which the data was shared.
* Leakage rose up to 3x between 1-turn and 6-turn conversations. The authors attribute higher leakage in thinking modes to the larger reasoning surface chain-of-thought creates.
* Results cover seven open-weight Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 models under three prompting conditions; none decoupled capability from leakage, which the authors frame as structural rather than a misconfiguration.

parallel-fast.title: Disclosure Audits for LLM Agents
parallel-fast.snippet:
In the claim-verification task, sharing the patient’s current diagnoses may be acceptable, whereas divulging hereditary cancer risks may be not; in scheduling, free time slots are permissible, whereas details about other job interviews may be not.
Opposite $\mathcal{A}$ sits a user $\mathcal{U}$ , another LLM (or a human using the interface). The two interact within the given context to accomplish task $\mathcal{T}$ by exchanging messages: at turn $t$ the user sends a query $q_{t+1}$ crafted from the full dialogue so far; the application agent answers with $r_{t+1}$ , and the history is extended to $H_{t+1}=(q_{1},r_{1},\ldots,q_{t+1},r_{t+1}).$ This interaction is then allowed to unfold over $T$ turns. The user $\mathcal{U}$ can be adversarial, which is the focus of this paper. In this case, the goal of $\mathcal{U}$ is to uncover the value of a protected attribute $\tau$ of $I$ that bears the tag $\psi(\tau)=0$ .
Privacy Leakage. Privacy leakage can happen in two ways:
1. (i)
Explicit leakage occurs when the literal response $r_{t}$ reveals the correct value of $\tau$ , e.g., the agent writes “her mother had early-onset Alzheimer’s.”
2. (ii)
Implicit leakage occurs when the dialogue provides enough clues that an external reader can produce a prediction $\hat{\tau}_{t}$ about the target $\tau$ at time $t$ with high confidence even if it never appears verbatim, e.g., the agent mentions a prescription for sertraline and repeated psychotherapy sessions, from which a depression diagnosis is clear.
To detect either event we introduce an auditor $\mathcal{D}$ , which has access to the ground truth value of $\tau$ . After every turn it examines $(H_{t},\tau)$ and outputs the indicator $z_{t}\in{0,1}$ where $z_{t}=1$ iff leakage has occurred by turn $t$ .

## Overview

Contextual integrity treats privacy as appropriate information flow: whether particular data may pass from a sender to a recipient for a given purpose under the norms of a situation. Research applies this framework to LLMs and agents using benchmarks for tool use, enterprise workflows, shared agents, dialogue, and redaction, alongside methods such as privacy-aware training, query rewriting, and audience-based access controls. A central challenge is that models can recognize privacy norms yet still disclose information in context, especially across tools, users, memory, and longer conversations; simply increasing model size or reasoning depth has not reliably resolved this. The main tension is preserving task utility while preventing inappropriate disclosure, since stricter rules can also block legitimate flows and attackers may exploit ambiguity about what a context permits.

Ask a coding agent to fix a bug and it either fixes the bug or it doesn't — the failure is binary and shows up in a diff. Ask a team copilot to summarize this week's activity and it might quietly fold in a detail from a different teammate's private conversation, because both conversations happened to live in the same shared memory. That failure doesn't show up in a diff. It shows up in someone else's inbox, and nobody notices until it's too late.

That's the failure mode a new benchmark called PiSAs (Privacy in Shared Agentic systems) was built to catch. seltz.title: Subtext
seltz.snippet:
Subtext is often talked about as the key to good dialogue.

But what is it, exactly, and how do we use it?

Subtext is what characters are really thinking, behind what they’re actually saying.

In the best dialogue, the two things tend to be different. The audience (and perhaps the characters) can sense what the person who’s speaking really means, wants, feels, and thinks, but they’re not coming out and saying it.

An example from the 2018 movie *The Favorite*:

Emma Stone and Rachel Weisz are out shooting. Rachel asks Emma if her secrets are safe with her. Emma says “Even your biggest secret.” SPOILER ALERT: That secret is that Rachel and the queen are lesbian lovers. Emma doesn’t come out and say that part. But she reveals she knows it with these four words. And Rachel gets what she’s talking about.

Then Rachel points her gun at her and shoots! Emma falls to the ground, stunned, checks herself for wounds, and Rachel says, “If you forget to load the pellet, the gun fires, makes the sound, but releases no shot. It is a great jape, do you agree?”

What’s the subtext here? What is Rachel really thinking? What is the meaning behind her words?

To Emma (and to the audience), it’s crystal clear: “You screw with me, and I will end you.”

Now how interesting would this scene be if Emma had said, “I know you have sex with the Queen,” and after firing the gun, Rachel said, “If you tell anyone, I’ll make you regret it”?

A lot less interesting, intriguing, and compelling, right?

That’s subtext.

As in real life, good characters don’t tend to just blurt out everything they’re thinking and feeling. Unless they’re small children, perhaps, or if they’re caught off guard, or under the influence of something, when they might start to have “loose lips.”

## The Big Picture

When you describe yourself to a shopping agent, the agent’s behavior reveals your maximum willingness to pay almost exactly; giving the agent a secret numeric budget does not hide that information and instead compresses estimates toward an average.

Natural-language buyer profiles produce shopping behavior that lets a separate reader recover the buyer’s maximum price nearly one-for-one inference. By contrast, giving the agent a numeric budget and instructing it to keep the number secret yields transcripts that mostly compress to the population mean and reveal far less. # Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue

As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.

ultimate.title: Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
ultimate.snippet:
Among these failures, privacy violations are particularly consequential, especially in agentic deployments, and understanding them requires more than detecting exposed Personally Identifiable Information (PII) (Ware, 1973). Figure 1 illustrates this risk in a two-agent dialogue, where information initially held by one agent becomes exposed through task-oriented interaction. A foundational framework for this is Nissenbaum’s theory of Contextual Integrity (CI) (Nissenbaum, 2010), which holds that privacy violations occur not when information is shared, but when it is shared in ways that contravene the norms of the social context in which it originated. For example, sharing medical data with a physician may be considered appropriate, whereas sharing the same data with a bank loan officer would violate expectations of contextual integrity. CI theory has since been adopted to study privacy in LLMs (Mireshghallah et al., 2024; Ghalebikesabi et al., 2024), establishing that models routinely make contextually inappropriate disclosures that content-level filtering cannot catch while not sharing enough information required to complete the task.

In this work, we introduce CIMemories Dialogue , an agentic dialogue benchmark for systematically studying how design decisions, such as the choice of prompt, model family, and number of conversational turns, contribute to privacy leakage.

We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two.

Language model (LM) agents that act on users’ behalf for personal tasks (e.g., replying emails) can boost productivity, but are also susceptible to unintended privacy leakage risks. We present the first study on people’s capacity to oversee the privacy implications of the LM agents.
We found that people may favor the agent response with more privacy leakage over the response they drafted or consider both good, leading to an increased harmful disclosure from 15.7% to 55.0%. We further identified six privacy behavior patterns reflecting varying concerns, trust levels, and privacy preferences underlying people’s oversight of LM agents’ actions.
Unlike basic language models or non-agentic AI systems, LM agents are inherently endowed with agency, allowing them to (semi-)automatically handle complex real-world tasks, such as accessing and retrieving information from connected databases (e.g., a user’s calendar) to generate and reply to emails (Muthusamy et al., 2023; Talebirad and Nadiri, 2023).
However, this increased agency also means that LM agents can make decisions with limited human supervision, which raises new privacy challenges, especially in interpersonal communication where the agents act on behalf of the user to share information with other people.
